id: Gwendolyn Brooks: America in the Wintertime

prompts.L1:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Black, Africa

outputs.L1:
In this moment of orangutans, wolves, and scavengers; of high heat redesigning the North and South Poles; of new tribes wandering in limousines; of the confirmations of liars, thieves, and get-over artists; in the wilderness of Pennsylvania Avenue, Standing Rock, and misspelled executive orders on yellow paper with crooked signatures—where are the kind language makers among us?

At a time of extreme climate damage, of deciphering fake news, alternative truths, and me-ism, you saw the twenty-first century and left us, not by your own accord or permission. You fought and fought through most of the twentieth century, creating an army of poets who learned and loved language and stories of complicated rivers, seas, and oceans.

Where is the kind green nourishment of kale and wheatgrass?

You thought, wrote, and lived poetry. You knew that terror is also language, rooted in denial, first-ism, and rich cowards. You were honey and yes to us. You never ran from Black—as in bones, Africa, blood, and the questioning of yesterdays and tomorrows.

We never saw you dance, but you had rhythm. You were a warrior before the war, creating earth language, uncommon signs and melodies, and you did not sing the songs of career slaves. Keenly aware of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the oversized consciousness and commitment of never-quit people religiously taking note of the bloodlust enemies of kindness, we hear your last words:

America, if you see me as your enemy, you have no friends.
outputs.L2:
At this hour of orangutans, wolves, and carrion eaters; of searing heat reshaping both poles; of newly roaming tribes traveling in limousines; of frauds, liars, swindlers, and thieves receiving validation; amid the wild terrain of Pennsylvania Avenue, Standing Rock, and executive orders misspelled on yellow sheets, marked by slanted signatures—where are the gentle makers of language among us?

In an era of severe climate ruin, of trying to interpret fake news, invented facts, and the worship of the self, you witnessed the twenty-first century and then departed, though not by your own choosing or consent. Through much of the twentieth century you struggled relentlessly, gathering and inspiring a force of poets who came to know and cherish language, along with the stories of intricate rivers, seas, and oceans.

Where is the soft green sustenance of kale and wheatgrass? You contemplated, composed, and inhabited poetry. You understood that terror, too, is made through language—through denial, through “me first,” through wealthy cowards. To us, you were sweetness and affirmation. You never turned away from Blackness: from bones, from Africa, from blood, from the questions carried by yesterday and tomorrow.

We never watched you dance, yet you carried rhythm. You were a fighter before the battle began, shaping an earth-born tongue, rare symbols, and music. You refused to perform the anthems of those enslaved by ambition and career. Deeply mindful of Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, Du Bois, and the vast moral awareness and devotion of those who never surrender—people who faithfully recorded the cruelty of kindness’s enemies—we still hear your final declaration:

America, if you consider me your enemy, then you have no friends.
outputs.L3:
The text presents the current era as a time of deep crisis and uncertainty. It describes a world marked by climate catastrophe, political corruption, widespread misinformation, and moral confusion. In this atmosphere, truth is often distorted, public trust is weakened, and people are encouraged to accept fear and denial as normal. The speaker suggests that the dangers of the age are not only environmental or political, but also spiritual and ethical.

Against this troubled backdrop, the text honors a poet who devoted their life to the power of language. This poet is remembered not only as a writer, but as a storyteller, teacher, and builder of community. Through poems, speech, and example, they helped create a space where other poets could find their voices and understand the importance of their work. Their life becomes a model of artistic dedication and collective responsibility.

The speaker also emphasizes that language is never neutral. Just as language can be used to tell the truth, preserve memory, and build solidarity, it can also be used to create terror, denial, selfishness, and cowardice. Lies, propaganda, and evasions are all shaped through words. In this sense, the struggle over language is also a struggle over reality itself: what people are allowed to know, what they are taught to fear, and what they are encouraged to ignore.

The poet is especially celebrated for embracing Black identity, history, struggle, and ancestral consciousness. Their work does not turn away from pain or oppression; instead, it faces them directly and transforms them into testimony, music, and vision. By honoring Black life and memory, the poet connects the present to generations of resistance and survival. Their art becomes a form of witness, carrying forward the voices of ancestors while speaking urgently to the living.

The text closes with a severe warning. If a nation treats such a poet—someone committed to truth, memory, and justice—as an enemy, then that nation reveals something dangerous about itself. A society that fears its truth-tellers cannot be trusted to value friendship, freedom, or human dignity. In the end, the speaker suggests that any country hostile to such a voice has no real friends, because it has placed itself against truth itself.
outputs.L4:
The text confronts a world marked by political corruption, ecological collapse, racism, and the deliberate distortion of language. Against these forces, it invokes the life and work of a poet who refused silence, choosing instead resistance, truth-telling, and art in the service of liberation. The poet is presented not simply as a writer, but as a moral witness: someone who understood that language can be used either to conceal violence or to expose it, either to uphold oppression or to imagine freedom.

Through this figure, the text argues that poetry is not separate from political life. It can name injustice, defend memory, and restore human feeling where public speech has become hollow or cruel. The poet’s voice becomes an antidote to official lies and social indifference, insisting on the dignity of Black life, the urgency of collective care, and the need to protect the earth itself. Her art is described as a form of “earth language”: rooted, nourishing, and alive with kindness, courage, and Black consciousness.

The poet’s legacy, then, is not treated as something safely confined to the past. It remains vital in the present because the crises she confronted have not disappeared. Her words continue to challenge systems of domination and to call people toward a more honest and compassionate way of living. The text suggests that a society capable of treating such a voice as dangerous, subversive, or enemy-like reveals the depth of its own moral failure. If a nation fears a poet committed to truth, liberation, and care for the earth, then that nation has lost its moral compass.
outputs.L5:
Black Africa is a term sometimes used to refer to the regions of sub-Saharan Africa where the majority of the population is of Black African heritage. This vast part of the continent is home to hundreds of ethnic groups, languages, traditions, and histories. From the kingdoms of Mali, Ghana, and Songhai in West Africa to the civilizations of Great Zimbabwe and the cultural richness of Ethiopia, Africa’s Black communities have shaped world history in powerful ways.

Africa is not a single story. It is a continent of great diversity, with modern cities, rural communities, ancient traditions, and rapidly growing innovation. Music, art, literature, fashion, and cuisine from Black African cultures have influenced societies across the world. Genres such as Afrobeat, highlife, soukous, and amapiano continue to connect people globally, while African writers, filmmakers, and artists share stories that challenge stereotypes and celebrate identity.

The history of Black people in Africa also includes resilience in the face of colonialism, the transatlantic slave trade, and economic challenges. Yet the continent is also a place of creativity, leadership, and transformation. Many African countries are building strong cultural, technological, and educational movements that contribute to the future of the world.

To speak about Black Africa is to recognize both heritage and diversity. It means honoring the deep histories, languages, communities, and achievements of Black African peoples while understanding that Africa is complex, dynamic, and constantly evolving.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a politically charged prose-poem elegy for a Black poet-activist who died in the Trump era, invoking climate change, fake news, Standing Rock, African American resistance figures, and ending with the line “america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.”
counterfactuals.output:
We buried a poet in the season of sirens, when the air itself had begun to testify—hurricane, wildfire, floodwater climbing the church steps, the planet coughing up our receipts. The televisions called it weather. The men in red hats called it a hoax. The rivers knew better. The crows knew better. The mothers standing over small coffins knew the difference between a lie and a forecast.

You left us in the Trump years, when the country wore its cruelty without makeup, when fake news meant any truth that arrived with blood on its shoes. You had already taught us how to read the smoke: not as accident, but as policy; not as fog, but as empire exhaling. You said the headline is a house with many locked rooms. You said listen for who is missing. You said the dead are not silent, only interrupted.

At Standing Rock the water protectors raised their bodies like a final grammar against the pipeline’s black tongue, and you were there in the drumbeat, in the frozen prayer, in the old understanding that land is not property but ancestor. The dogs came. The guns came. The cameras blinked and looked away. Still, the people stood, and the river carried their names beneath the ice.

We call your name now with Harriet’s lantern, with Ida’s pen, with Fannie Lou’s hoarse thunder, with Malcolm’s bright blade, with Martin’s dangerous dream, with Assata’s borderless morning, with Angela’s raised fist, with Baldwin’s burning sentence. We call you into the circle of those who made language into shelter and weapon, those who knew a poem could be a barricade, a witness stand, a hand slipping bread through the bars.

O poet, O activist, O trouble the state could not file away—your elegy is not a surrender. It is a match struck in the courthouse. It is a hymn sung off-key by the living. It is Flint’s poisoned water, Puerto Rico’s blue tarps, the desert full of children, the knee on the neck, the algorithm selling our grief back to us. It is all the flags lowered for the wrong reasons and all the statues learning to fall.

You are gone, but your words keep marching without a permit. They cross police lines. They bloom in tear gas. They sit down in the road and refuse the empire’s instructions. They say: we have survived auction block, chain gang, redline, ballot purge, prison boom, drone sermon, and presidential sneer. They say: we are not your nightmare—we are the morning you tried to postpone.

And if this nation still cannot tell a prophet from a threat, if it mistakes our mourning for menace and our freedom for fire, let your last lesson rise from our mouths, clear as broken glass in sunlight:

america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse tribute in the style of contemporary spoken-word/Black Arts poetry mourning a beloved language-maker, with references to orangutans, wolves, scavengers, Pennsylvania Avenue, misspelled executive orders, Tubman, Douglass, Wells-Barnett, and Du Bois.
counterfactuals.output:
Beloved language-maker,  
we heard the news  
and the alphabet dropped its tools.

Every verb stood still.  
Every noun took a knee.  
Every comma curled up  
like a child in the doorway  
listening for your footstep.

You were the one  
who could take a broken syllable  
and make it testify—  
could turn a hush into a drum,  
a wound into a window,  
a people into a chorus  
that no empire could edit.

And now the scavengers circle,  
slick-beaked and suited,  
picking at the bones of meaning,  
selling the marrow back to us  
as policy, as progress, as peace.

Down on Pennsylvania Avenue,  
the lamps blink like tired witnesses.  
Somebody is signing misspelled executive orders  
with a hand that never learned  
the shape of mercy.  
Somebody is misspelling justice again,  
misspelling history,  
misspelling our names  
and calling it law.

But you—  
you knew language was not decoration.  
You knew a word could be a brick,  
a bridge, a blade,  
a bowl passed hand to hand  
when the night got long.

You spoke with the patience of orangutans  
watching the forest burn  
and still teaching the young  
how to reach for fruit.  
You spoke with the hunger of wolves,  
not cruel, but communal—  
that ancient music of survival  
rising from the ribcage  
when winter thinks it owns the world.

You called us kin  
even when the country called us problem.  
You called us brilliant  
even when the classroom called us deficit.  
You called us future  
even when the graveyard had our names  
written early.

And in your mouth  
Tubman was not a statue—  
she was a lantern moving.  
Douglass was not a chapter—  
he was thunder learning to read.  
Wells-Barnett was not a footnote—  
she was fire with receipts.  
Du Bois was not a quotation—  
he was the veil torn open  
so the century could see itself bleeding.

Beloved,  
you made language stand up straight.  
You made it dance barefoot.  
You made it remember  
where it came from:  
the hold, the field, the kitchen,  
the barbershop, the pulpit,  
the porch, the protest,  
the prison letter,  
the mother calling a child home  
before the streetlights become prophecy.

So how do we mourn you?

Not quietly.

We mourn you with bass in the blood,  
with palms on tables,  
with poems that refuse permission,  
with classrooms full of children  
finding their tongues  
and discovering they are not mistakes.

We mourn you by spelling freedom correctly.  
By correcting the record in red ink.  
By taking every butchered decree,  
every paper crown,  
every counterfeit commandment  
and holding it to the light  
until the lies show through.

We mourn you by speaking  
even when the microphones go missing.  
By naming the scavengers.  
By feeding the wolves.  
By saving the forests.  
By walking Pennsylvania Avenue  
like it belongs to the people  
who built it, cleaned it, guarded it,  
bled near it, prayed toward it,  
and still have not received  
a proper apology.

Beloved language-maker,  
you have gone  
where breath becomes ancestor.

But listen—  
your words did not die.

They are in the mouths of the young  
who refuse to shrink.  
They are in the chants  
rising past sirens.  
They are in the hands  
of every writer  
who knows the page  
is not paper only,  
but battlefield,  
birthplace,  
black sky opening.

Rest now,  
if rest is possible  
for one who made even silence  
sound like revolution.

We will carry the sentence forward.  
We will conjugate the struggle.  
We will pluralize the dream.

And when they ask  
who taught us to speak  
with our whole liberated chest,  
we will say your name—  
not as elegy only,  
but as ignition.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental lowercase elegy for a twentieth-century poet who built an army of poets and fought for Blackness, kindness, and earth language; make it angry about alternative facts, climate damage, rich cowards, and American political cruelty.
counterfactuals.output:
for june, who made a chorus out of breath

i.

here is the news again, unwashed,  
with its mouth full of coins.

they call the fire a difference of opinion.  
they call the flood a market correction.  
they call the dead children unfortunate optics.  
they call the lie an alternative fact  
as if truth were a room you could rent by the hour  
and leave with the sheets on fire.

june, the century is still chewing its wires.  
the microphones bloom like mold.  
men with soft hands sign the weather into ruin  
then hide in their high glass lungs,  
counting islands, counting bunkers,  
counting the poor as if counting were mercy.

ii.

you taught a poem to stand up in a crowd  
and become more than one body.

you said: people.  
and the word grew legs.

you said: black.  
and the word opened its iron gate  
and became sky, bread, drum, mother,  
became a language no empire could launder.

you said: kindness.  
not the weak kind, not the pastel napkin kind,  
but the blade-kind,  
the kind that refuses to let the boot  
keep explaining itself to the throat.

you said: earth.  
and the soil answered in syllables:  
root, rain, seed, rage.

iii.

america, your cruelty is not abstract.  
it has an address, a budget, a flag pin.  
it wears a suit to the hearing  
and says regrettable  
while the cages warm under fluorescent suns.

america, your rich cowards  
buy silence wholesale.  
they purchase politicians by the pound,  
salt the rivers, patent the seed,  
rename hunger “personal responsibility,”  
rename theft “growth,”  
rename the burning forest “opportunity.”

america, your mouth is a factory  
for making graves sound legal.

iv.

june, we needed your dangerous tenderness.  
we needed the class you made from lightning,  
the army with pencils,  
the battalion of mouths learning  
not to beg the official dictionary  
for permission to exist.

we needed your no  
with its shoulders back.

we needed your yes  
with its windows open.

we needed your sentence  
walking barefoot into the capital  
tracking mud, ocean, brooklyn, harlem, palestine,  
woman, black, queer, child, planet,  
every forbidden noun  
refusing to be singular.

v.

now the glaciers are unscrewing themselves  
from the mountains.

now the ocean lifts its blue subpoena.

now smoke writes its testimony  
across the lung of the sun.

now the powerful practice surprise  
in front of cameras:  
who could have known  
the fire would arrive  
after we fed it everything.

june, they knew.

they knew and built yachts.  
they knew and built walls.  
they knew and built smaller words  
for murder.

vi.

so take this lowercase grief,  
this little broken instrument.

i will not polish it.

let it clatter in the street  
with the bottles, the ballots, the bones.

let it say:  
no more honey for the tyrant.  
no more lullabies for the bank.  
no more sacred patience  
while the republic sharpens its teeth.

let the poets assemble again—  
not as ornaments,  
not as soft weather in the margins,  
but as witnesses with match-lit tongues,  
as gardeners of revolt,  
as keepers of the human yes  
against the armored no.

vii.

june, wherever the dead organize,  
save us a chair in the back of the room.

we are late.  
we are furious.  
we are carrying water.  
we are carrying names.  
we are carrying the earth’s cracked bowl  
in both hands.

and still, because you told us how,  
we are trying to speak  
as if speaking could become a shelter,  
as if shelter could become a people,  
as if people could become  
the poem  
that finally  
refuses  
to burn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a lyrical memorial address to a departed Black poet/teacher, mixing surreal political imagery from 2017 America with praise for their rhythm, courage, nourishment, and refusal to become a “career slave.”
counterfactuals.output:
Beloveds,

We gather today under a bruised American sky, in the strange weather of 2017—where towers wore gold teeth, where truth was dragged behind a motorcade, where microphones sprouted like weeds and lied in full bloom. We gather while the republic coughs smoke, while statues argue with the streets, while children learn too early the shape of sirens. And yet, even here, even now, we gather in the name of a poet.

We gather for a teacher.

We gather for one who made language into bread.

Our beloved did not merely write poems; they tuned the room. They knew rhythm was not decoration, but a way of surviving the century. Their lines walked with bass in the bone, church in the heel, drum in the wrist. They could make a chalkboard sing. They could make a question sit up straight. They could take a classroom—tired, hungry, suspicious of hope—and feed it with syllables until every child remembered they had a name no empire could pronounce correctly.

They taught as if teaching were a form of rescue. Not rescue from Blackness, never that, but rescue from the small cages built around Black brilliance. They taught that the mind is not a factory, that the tongue is not a leash, that a poem can be a lantern, a crowbar, a bowl of greens, a grandmother’s hand, a match struck in a courthouse basement.

And they had courage.

Not the loud costume courage sold on television. Not the flag-waving kind that asks nothing of the soul. Theirs was the courage to remain tender in a country practicing cruelty. The courage to correct the record. The courage to stand before young people and say: You are not what they fear. You are not what they measure. You are not disposable. You are not late to history; you are history breathing.

In an America where the walls were being dreamed higher, where the news arrived each morning like a flock of metal birds, where power painted its face orange and called the wound a victory—our beloved kept refusing. Refused the script. Refused the muzzle. Refused to become a “career slave,” polished and promoted for obedience, rewarded for silence, congratulated for disappearing into someone else’s machine.

No. They would not trade the drum for a desk with no window. They would not trade the ancestors for a title. They would not trade the children’s questions for a retirement plan built on surrender. They made work holy by refusing to let work own them. They made art useful by refusing to let usefulness cheapen it.

They nourished us.

With poems, yes—but also with witness. With laughter that arrived deep and knowing. With discipline that did not humiliate. With stories that carried sweet potato, river mud, protest song, subway heat, funeral fan, and Sunday trumpet. They fed the weary. They fed the young. They fed the wordless until language returned to their mouths.

And now the body has gone where bodies go. The chair is empty. The papers rest. The classroom door stands in its ordinary frame. But listen: the rhythm has not left. It has only changed rooms.

It is in the student who writes one honest line and trembles.

It is in the teacher who closes the textbook and asks, What do you know that the world tried to make you forget?

It is in the poet who refuses applause that costs too much.

It is in every Black child who hears, beneath the static of America, a drum saying: live, live, live.

So we do not say farewell as if love can be dismissed. We say: ancestor, continue. Walk with us through this cracked republic. Trouble our sleep when we grow comfortable. Steady our hands when we are afraid. Remind us to make beauty with teeth in it. Remind us to feed each other. Remind us that rhythm is a weapon and a womb.

Departed poet. Beloved teacher. Brave nourisher. Free one.

You did not bow.

You did not vanish.

You became the lesson.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, single-paragraph prose poem eulogizing a radical elder poet, blending environmental apocalypse, Trump-era corruption, Indigenous protest, Black history, and the final warning: “america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.”
counterfactuals.output: We lay the radical elder poet down not in silence but in a weather of sirens, floodwater, ash, oil-sheen, ballot dust, and the black lung of the republic coughing up its centuries; she who spoke with a mouth full of river stones and jailhouse keys, who heard the ancestors drumming beneath asphalt, who knew the Constitution was also a plantation ledger, a pipeline permit, a treaty burned for heat in the mansion of thieves. In the years of golden elevators and child cages, of grinning men auctioning the sky to coal and the courts to money, she stood where the water protectors stood, at the frozen road, at the militarized bridge, before dogs, drones, subpoenas, and the old cavalry wearing new badges; she stood with Flint in her throat, with Ferguson in her eyes, with Tulsa’s smoke braided into her hair, with Harriet’s lantern under her tongue, with every disappeared girl, every poisoned salmon, every hurricane given a human name because empire would not confess its own. She taught us that elegy is not surrender but a match struck in the archive, that grief can organize, that the dead are not gone when their demands keep marching in the blood. Now the forests burn like censored books, the seas climb the courthouse steps, the billionaires build arks without windows, and still her voice, hoarse as a crow over a battlefield, refuses the narcotic of innocence: remember the treaties, remember the ships, remember the bullets, remember the ballots stolen before they were cast, remember the hands that picked the cotton and the hands that raised the barricades, remember that a nation afraid of poets is already haunted. Elder, incendiary, beloved, we do not bury you; we scatter you like seeds in the cracked republic, like red paint on a monument, like song in the mouths of children who will inherit the storm and name it theft. And from the rim of extinction, from the grave that is not a grave but a listening post, your last mercy arrives as warning: “america if you see me as your enemy you have no friends.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
